name: Cervical traction

lead: Cervical traction applies a gentle pulling force to the neck, in a clinic or with a home device. Posture-focused users try it hoping to ease a forward head position and improve neck curve and profile.

The chain is the neck gently stretched, neck tension eased, then the head carried further back. Physical therapists use it mainly for neck pain with nerve-root symptoms such as cervical radiculopathy. Guideline evidence is described as low quality, and some reviews report short-term pain relief when traction is added to physiotherapy. No study of appearance was found.

paras: Sessions are done with clinic equipment or home over-door and inflatable devices, usually for short periods repeated over weeks. In physio it is typically combined with exercise.
The reviewed sources do not detail risks. Neck symptoms can have other causes, so people with persistent pain, numbness or weakness may want to see a clinician before using it.

angle.text: Posture-focused users try cervical traction to ease a forward head position and improve neck curve and profile. The path runs from a gentle neck stretch to eased tension to the head carried further back. Physiotherapists use it for nerve-root neck pain; its effect on posture appearance has not been tested.

lead: Cervical traction applies a gentle pulling force to the neck, by hand in a clinic or with a mechanical or home device, to open space between vertebrae and ease pressure on neck structures. Physical therapists use it mainly for neck pain with nerve-root symptoms (cervical radiculopathy), often alongside exercise and manual therapy.[1][2][3]

In looksmaxxing and posture circles, neck traction devices are discussed as a way to restore the neck's natural curve and reduce forward-head posture, the pattern in which the head sits ahead of the shoulders and the chin juts forward.[4] A neater neck line and a head stacked over the shoulders change how the jaw, neck and profile read, which is the appearance goal people attach to the devices.

Research on cervical traction concerns pain and function rather than posture aesthetics. A 2018 meta-analysis of randomized trials found significant effects of mechanical traction on pain and disability when added to physical therapy for cervical radiculopathy, while review articles describe the underlying evidence base as limited and varied.[2][5]

paras: Traction is a family of techniques for relieving pressure on the spine or aligning bones, and orthopedic medicine describes skin and skeletal forms; illustrated traction devices appear as early as a Greek device of the 2nd century AD in a Byzantine edition of Galen.[1] Cervical traction applies the same idea to the neck, delivered manually by a therapist or mechanically with a pulley, air or over-door set-up.[2][5]

Reviews of cervical radiculopathy list traction among the conservative options, along with immobilization, anti-inflammatory medication, physical therapy and epidural injections, with at least six weeks of conservative care typical before surgery is considered.[6]

Forward head posture is described as the head carried ahead of the shoulders with a rounded upper back, so that the earlobes sit forward of the shoulders and the chin projects.[4] The general treatment advice in reference sources centers on strengthening the deep neck flexors and mid-back, stretching tight neck and upper-trapezius muscles, mobilizing stiff thoracic joints and adjusting ergonomics.[4] Traction devices are discussed in these communities as a way to add a decompression or stretch component to that routine.
No studies found on cervical traction for posture appearance.

For neck pain, a 2018 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials in cervical radiculopathy reported that mechanical traction had significant effects on pain at short and intermediate follow-up and on disability at intermediate term when added to other physical therapy, with the quality of evidence assessed using GRADE.[2] Wikipedia summarizes a 2018 meta-analysis reporting reduced pain with added traction, a 2020 study favoring mechanical over manual traction, and a 2017 review that rated guideline support as low quality; researchers have suggested inconsistent dosage across studies may explain conflicting results.[1]

A 2009 multicenter randomized trial examined manual therapy, exercise and traction for radiculopathy, noting that evidence for mechanical traction had been limited.[3] A 2021 double-blinded randomized trial of 66 patients compared cervical traction with and without neural mobilization on pain, function and disability.[7] A 1982 physiotherapy paper also reviews neck traction.[8]

Reviews of radiculopathy stress that symptoms must correlate with the underlying pathology and that neck symptoms can have varied causes, including heart-mimicking presentations, so evaluation by a clinician is part of standard care.[6][9] Detailed adverse-event data for home traction devices were not found.
